newsitem.title: USA: Nine feet of snow in Sierra Nevada, train derailed.
newsitem.headline: Nine feet of snow in Sierra Nevada, train derailed.

text.p: Residents of the Sierra Nevada began to dig out on Monday from a powerful storm that dumped near-record snowfall, stranding thousands of travelers and knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes.
Up to nine feet of snow has fallen since Friday in some parts of the popular Lake Tahoe ski resort area on the northern California-Nevada border.
"It just kept on pouring in," said National Weather Service meteorologist Rick Canepa, adding that the amount of snowfall may set a record for the Sierras.
The heavy snow caused major transportation problems.

Amtrak's California Zephyr, travelling from Chicago to Oakland, California, partially derailed in heavy snow and ice late Sunday about 40 miles north of Sacramento, with 118 passengers aboard, Amtrak said. It took crews about 12 hours to get the train back on the tracks.
None of the passengers or crew was hurt, an Amtrak spokesman said. After several hours delay, the passengers were placed on buses to complete their trip.
Light snow continued to fall Monday, but weather forecasters said the worst had past.
With the conditions improving, rescue teams were able to launch a search for two cross-country skiers missing since Friday in the Sierra Nevada mountains.

About 21,500 Pacific Gas & Electric Co. customers in the Sierra foothills remained without power Monday due to the heavy snowfall, PG&E spokesman Cory Warren said. The majority of those affected should have their power restored by Christmas Eve, he said.
PG&E said crews wearing snowshoes hiked the Sierra foothills, looking for downed power lines. Other crews were patrolling the area in snowcats, similar to snowmobiles.
"We are dealing with very rugged back country. Our crews are working in deep forest and deep snow," Bill Sessa, PG&E spokesman, said.
Since Friday the blustery storm has affected nearly 96,000 PG&E customers in the Sierras.

The heavy snow forced the closure of some highways through the mountains between California and Nevada. Road closures in the Lake Tahoe area stranded thousands of residents and travelers, South Lake Tahoe police dispatcher Sue Dickey said.
"Many cars were stranded, but the roads are improving," Dickey said.
Highways and roads buried by the snow were being cleared and many were reopened Monday, allowing motorists to pass, the California Highway Patrol said.

Highway 50, which links Sacramento, California, to Carson City, Nevada, should fully re-open Monday following a two-day partial closure due to snow slides and zero visibility. The largest of the slides covered the road with snow 20 feet deep and 100 feet long. Highway officials used propane and oxygen cannons to bring down snow above the mountain highway.

Over the weekend, gusting winds from the powerful storm knocked down poles and power lines, causing scattered power outages along the northern California coast and causing problems for last-minute holiday shoppers and travelers.
Marble-size hail was reported in the San Francisco Bay area and Napa County officials said a small tornado touched down Sunday in wine country.
